title: Goldman raises 2030 data-center forecast to 273 GW, implying $8.5T capex
subtitle: A note to clients lifts global capacity projections 26% above the July baseline, with AI workloads accounting for most of the new gigawatts and projects above 75 MW taking two-thirds of the build.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Goldman Sachs raised its 2030 global data-center capacity forecast to 273 GW in a note published November 2 and distributed November 3. The new number is 26% above its July estimate of 217 GW. Baseline 2025 capacity is roughly 103 GW, which implies an average annual growth rate of 21%. Over five years, that works out to about 170 GW of new capacity. At an assumed cost of roughly $50 billion per gigawatt — covering land, shell, power infrastructure, cooling, and compute — the implied capital spending is about $8.5 trillion. The note attributes the upgrade to AI infrastructure demand, with AI-focused cloud providers and GPU-hosting facilities contributing 11.8 GW to the 2026–2030 outlook.

The near-term pace matters as much as the 2030 number. Goldman expects roughly 25 GW added in 2026, 32 GW in 2027, and 35 GW in 2028. The step-up in 2027–2028 lines up with the Nvidia Vera Rubin and AMD Helios delivery schedules, the hyperscaler 20-year lease commitments signed through 2026, and the Apollo-arranged financings announced for SpaceX and Anthropic. Projects of at least 75 MW — the hyperscale and AI-training class — are projected to account for 66% of the global additions, compared with a historical share closer to 40%. The buildout is concentrating.

The forecast is an industry outlook, not a certainty. The two obvious downside risks are power and politics. Grid interconnect queues in PJM, ERCOT, and MISO already stretch into the early 2030s for projects above 500 MW, and new generation is not coming online at the pace the capacity curve assumes. The November 3 ballot measures — 37 of 41 against new data-center development — add a second risk that was not priced into the July baseline. A third, quieter risk is the trajectory of model efficiency: a 10x drop in inference cost per token over the next eighteen months, which several labs are now targeting, would cut the training and serving GW curve meaningfully.

A note for learners: $8.5 trillion is roughly 8% of global GDP, spread over five years. A number that large is best read as a direction, not a prediction. The useful question is not 'will it be 273 GW or 240 GW,' which no one can answer, but 'what has to be true for the forecast to hold.' That gives you a short list of observables — permitting throughput, HV transformer delivery times, chip supply, model-efficiency improvements, utility rate cases — that you can actually watch month to month. Anyone whose job touches this buildout, from a city planner to a quant, benefits from tracking those observables directly rather than taking the headline at face value.
